'''''Brugmansia aurea''''', also known as '''golden angel's trumpet''',<ref name = "COL">''Brugmansia aurea'' Lagerh. (n.d.-b). Catalogue of Life. Retrieved May 30, 2026, from https://www.catalogueoflife.org/data/taxon/NFCP</ref><ref name = "REPAD">Holmes, B. (n.d.). ''Brugmansia aurea'' Lagerh. (1893:33). The Recently Extinct Plants and Animals Database. Retrieved May 30, 2026, from https://recentlyextinctspecies.com/solanales-tomatoes-potatoes-eggplants-nightshades-etc/brugmansia-aurea</ref> is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the nightshade family [[Solanaceae]] that was native to Ecuador and Colombia,<ref name = "POWO" /> but is now [[Extinct in the Wild]].<ref name="iucn status 15 November 2021" /><ref name = "REPAD" /> Despite being declared extinct in its native range, ''Brugmansia aurea'' is a popular ornamental and is widely cultivated, like the other members of its genus. 

==Description==
[[File:Brugmansia aurea (Solanaceae) Nationale Plantentuin Meise 10-01-2010 14-01-52.JPG|thumb|right|''Brugmansia aurea'' cultivated in the [[Meise Botanic Garden]]]]
===Vegetative characteristics===
''Brugmansia aurea'' is an up to 8 m tall shrub or small tree<ref name = "Giardi & Fried, 2026" /> with spreading or drooping, almost smooth branches and smooth, grey bark.<ref name = "Lagerheim, 1893" /> The leaves are glabrous or nearly glabrous.<ref name = "De Lorenzo Cáceres, 2003" />
===Generative characteristics===
The axillary, tubular, pendent, sulphur yellow to golden yellow, pleasantly fragrant, nectariferous flowers have 7–8 cm long, smooth pedicels.<ref name = "Lagerheim, 1893" /> The tubular, 13–16 cm long calyx with a pubescent outer surface is divided into 2–5 lobes at the apex.<ref name = "Lagerheim, 1893" /> The yellow, 15–18 cm long corolla bears five 5–6 cm long,<ref name = "Lagerheim, 1893" /> recurved teeth.<ref name = "De Lorenzo Cáceres, 2003">De Lorenzo Cáceres, J. M. S. (2003). Las especies del género ''Brugmansia'' cultivadas en España. Arboles Ornamentales. Retrieved May 31, 2026, from https://www.arbolesornamentales.es/Brugmansia.htm</ref> The stamens are 14.5 cm long.<ref name = "Lagerheim, 1893" />

==Taxonomy==
''Brugmansia aurea'' {{au|Lagerh.}} was published by [[Gustaf Lagerheim|Nils Gustaf Lagerheim]] in 1893.<ref name = "Lagerheim, 1893">Lagerheim, N. G. (1893). [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/40103202 Eine neue, goldgelbe ''Brugmansia'' (''B. aurea'' Lagerh.).] Gartenflora (Vol. 42, p. 33).</ref><ref name = "IPNI">''Brugmansia aurea'' Lagerh. (n.d.). International Plant Names Index. Retrieved May 31, 2026, from https://www.ipni.org/n/37434-2</ref> However, ''Brugmansia aurea'' {{au|Harrison}} had already been published by Harrison<!-- What is the complete name? --> in 1837, making the later publication of ''Brugmansia aurea'' {{au|Lagerh.}} illegitimate.<ref name = "Hay, 2021">Hay, A. (2021). [https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Alistair-Hay/publication/349480248_2802_Proposal_to_conserve_the_name_Brugmansia_aurea_Lagerh_against_B_aurea_Harrison_Solanaceae/links/603eca7c4585154e8c72463d/2802-Proposal-to-conserve-the-name-Brugmansia-aurea-Lagerh-against-B-aurea-Harrison-Solanaceae.pdf (2802) Proposal to conserve the name ''Brugmansia aurea'' Lagerh. against ''B. aurea'' Harrison (Solanaceae).] Taxon, 70(1), 212-213.</ref> As ''Brugmansia aurea'' {{au|Lagerh.}} had been widely used, it was proposed to conserve it against ''Brugmansia aurea'' {{au|Harrison}}.<ref name = "Hay, 2021" />
It is placed in the section [[Brugmansia sect. Brugmansia|''Brugmansia'' sect. ''Brugmansia'']].<ref name = "Hay & Gottschalk, n.d.">Hay, A., & Gottschalk, M. (n.d.). Arten. GdS-Fachgruppen Dahlien, Fuchsien Und Kübelpflanzen. Retrieved April 25, 2026, from https://www.ddfgg.de/brugmansien/brugmansien_arten.php</ref>
===Etymology===
The [[binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] ''aurea'' means "golden".<ref name=RHSLG>{{cite book | last=Harrison |first=Lorraine | title=RHS Latin for Gardeners | year=2012 |publisher=Mitchell Beazley | location=United Kingdom | isbn=978-1-84533-731-5}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
It was native to the Andes from south-central Ecuador to northeast Colombia at elevations of 2000–3000 m above sea level.<ref name="iucn status 15 November 2021" /> It grew mainly in Andean cloud forests and damp ravines with a subtropical mountainous climate, characterised by high humidity, moderate temperatures and frequent fog.<ref name = "Giardi & Fried, 2026" />
It has been introduced into Italy,<ref name = "Giardi & Fried, 2026" /><ref name = "POWO" /> Rwanda,<ref name = "POWO" /> France (Southern Corsica), and Spain.<ref name = "Giardi & Fried, 2026">Giardi, L., & Fried, G. (2026) [https://sbocc.fr/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Carnets-botaniques-n%C2%B0304.pdf Brugmansia aurea Lagerh., a newly introduced species in Southern Corsica.] Carnets botaniques Article n° 304 – 13 mai 2026</ref> 

==Ecology==
The very fragrant, trumpet-shaped flowers attract bees, butterflies, and birds.<ref name = "Laface et al., 2020">Laface, V. L. A., Musarella, C. M., Cano Ortiz, A., Quinto Canas, R., Cannavò, S., & Spampinato, G. (2020). Three New Alien Taxa for Europe and a Chorological Update on the Alien Vascular Flora of Calabria (Southern Italy). Plants, 9(9), 1181. https://doi.org/10.3390/plants9091181 </ref> The flowers are pollinated by the hummingbird ''[[Ensifera ensifera]]''.<!-- Source says Docimastes ensifer --><ref name = "Lagerheim, 1893" /> The floral tube is very often pierced by short-billed, [[nectar robbing]] hummingbirds.<ref name = "Lagerheim, 1893" />

==Conservation==
No natural wild populations are known and ''Brugmansia aurea'' is now [[Extinct in the Wild]].<ref name="iucn status 15 November 2021" /> It is threatened by [[Introgressive hybridization in plants |introgressive hybridisation]] with ''[[Brugmansia versicolor]]'', via the hybrid [[Brugmansia × candida|''Brugmansia'' × ''candida'']].<ref name="iucn status 15 November 2021" />

==Cultivation==
[[File:Golden Angel's Trumpet in Athens on May 2, 2023.jpg|thumb|right|Two ''Brugmansia aurea'' seen from below]]
''Brugmansia aurea'' is cultivated as an ornamental plant.<ref name = "Laface et al., 2020" /> Several [[cultivar]]s exist, notably 'Grand Marnier' with peach-coloured flowers. As with other members of its genus, it cannot handle temperatures below {{cvt|5|C|F|abbr=on}}, but in colder climates can be placed outside in a sheltered spot during the summer months.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/115966/brugmansia-aurea-grand-marnier/details | title = ''Brugmansia aurea'' 'Grand Marnier' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 7 September 2021}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Angel's Trumpet, Brugmansia |url=https://hort.extension.wisc.edu/articles/angels-trumpet-brugmansia/ |access-date=2024-01-14 |website=Wisconsin Horticulture |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Toxicity==
All parts of the plant are poisonous.<ref>"[http://www.bhg.com/gardening/plant-dictionary/annual/angels-trumpet/ Angel's Trumpet]," The Better Homes and Gardens Plant Encyclopedia.</ref>

== Uses ==
It is used as a [[hallucinogen]]. Its most potent cultivar is ''Culebra Borrachero'', which has a high concentration of the psychoactive [[scopolamine]].<ref name="Pratt2007">{{cite book|first=Christina |last=Pratt|chapter=Brugmansia Aurea|title=An Encyclopedia of Shamanism|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HltJMMq1_60C&pg=PA68|year=2007|publisher=[[Rosen Publishing]]|isbn=978-1-4042-1040-0|pages=68–70}}</ref> It has also been used as a [[truth serum]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=House |first1=Robert E. |title=The Use of Scopolamine in Criminology |journal=The American Journal of Police Science |volume=2 |issue=4 |pages=328–336 |date=1931 |doi=10.2307/1147361 |issn=1547-6154 |jstor=1147361 |df=mdy-all }}</ref> Borrachero loosely translates to "get-you-drunk", and scopolamine is also known as Devil's Breath<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Draper |first1=Lucy |title=Does the 'Devil's Breath' Drug Really Exist? |work=Newsweek |date=2015-09-03 |url=http://europe.newsweek.com/does-devils-breath-drug-really-exist-332465 |access-date=2017-04-13 |df=mdy-all }}</ref> and burundanga.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Cotroneo |first1=Christian |title=The World's Scariest Drug |work=[[The Huffington Post]] |date=2013-09-03 |url=http://www.huffingtonpost.ca/2013/09/03/devils-breath-scopolamine_n_3860318.html |access-date=2017-04-13 |df=mdy-all }}</ref>
